articles.title: Israel claims control of Lebanon’s key Ali al-Taher ridge: What that means
articles.summary: Israeli Defence Ministry asserts operational control over strategic highland; Hezbollah yet to comment.
articles.body:
Israel this week has claimed to have established operational control over the strategically vital Ali al-Taher ridge in southern Lebanon, after an extended operation against positions of the Lebanese armed group Hezbollah.

In a statement on Friday, Defence Minister Israel Katz claimed Israeli forces had driven Hezbollah fighters out of what he said was a network of tunnels ⁠⁠under the contested highland, 15km (10 miles) from the border.

“Prime Minister Netanyahu and I are leading a clear and uncompromising policy, reinforced every day by the [Israeli military]: Israel will not withdraw from the security zone in Lebanon until Hezbollah is disarmed throughout Lebanon and the threats to the residents of the Galilee are removed,” he was quoted as saying by Israeli media. “The capture of Ali Taher is an important step towards achieving this goal.”

Iran-backed Hezbollah has yet to formally comment on the Israeli claims. However, hours before Katz’s comments, Reuters news agency reported that Iran had warned the United States last month that it would respond forcefully if Israeli attacks on the ridge, which rises 600 metres above sea level (1,970 feet), continued.

Israel and Hezbollah have been fighting, with varying levels of intensity, since October 2023. Israel has twice escalated the conflict – first in September 2024 and then in March this year, following the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran.

Israel has been working to embed its occupation of southern Lebanon since the latest escalation, when it announced the creation of a “security” or “buffer” zone, which rights groups say has involved the deliberate destruction of civilian infrastructure – potentially a war crime – and is responsible for the displacement of hundreds of thousands of Lebanese.

Israeli strikes and ground operations around the Ali al-Taher ridge continued despite a ceasefire agreed in June, after Israel gained control of nearby Beaufort Castle and part of the higher ground overlooking much of southern Lebanon and northern Israel.

According to Mohanad Hage Ali, of the Carnegie Middle East Centre, Israel’s success has partly been down to technological superiority but also due to the complete absence of “inhibition” in their assaults upon Lebanese towns and villages, which have often accrued daily casualty rates of dozens of people.

“There aren’t any consequences to their actions,” he said. “They can demolish entire villages and wipe out whole societies in a way they could never do before. It’s ethnic cleansing.”

Pitched as a measure to protect citizens of northern Israel, who Israeli analysts such as Ori Goldberg described as being owed an electoral debt by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of crucial elections later this year, the occupation is also a means of exerting additional pressure on the government in Beirut.

“The Israeli ‘operational control’ over the ridge is no doubt a tactical, even strategic, gain, enabling Israel a better control over southern Lebanon,” said Ahron Bregman, an Israeli security analyst and senior teaching fellow at King’s College London. “From an Israeli perspective, it is a way to put pressure on the Lebanese government: Tackle Hezbollah head-on, or we stay here.”

Nicholas Blanford, a non-resident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council and an authority on the group, said Hezbollah’s lack of comment on the Israeli claims raised a number of questions.

“It could be that a deal’s been done. It could be that Israel is exaggerating what it means by ‘operational control’,” he said, noting that neither the extent of Israel’s military control over the ridge, nor the infrastructure contained within it, is known.

“What we do know is that Hezbollah appears ready to get back into the resistance business, but no longer seems to be making the decisions,” he said. “Those are coming from Iran, who appear to want to keep things quiet for now.”

Analysts also suggested that a lack of a response from Tehran may frustrate Netanyahu, who has invested much of his electoral stock in finishing the war with Iran, an opponent he has characterised as posing an existential threat to the country since at least the early 1990s.

Katz has described an attack against Israel as freeing its military “from all constraints”, and that in such a scenario, the military would “strike all infrastructure – including energy infrastructure – and return Iran to the Stone Age and darkness”, all of which would almost certainly constitute war crimes.

However, how far Israel – diplomatically, economically and militarily dependent upon the US – can proceed beyond rhetoric is open to question.

With Netanyahu predicted to struggle in October’s elections, what happens in southern Lebanon may prove crucial.

“Will Iran come to Hezbollah’s aid?” Bregman asked. “One person for sure – a certain Benjamin Netanyahu prays that they do – as it could even postpone the forthcoming elections in Israel in which, if judged by current polls, he will be defeated.”

images.caption: Smoke rises following Israeli strikes on the strategically important Ali al-Taher ridge in southern Lebanon [File: AFP]

Defence Minister Israel Katz, who faces re-election later this year, has threatened to “return Iran to the Stone Age” if it responds to Israel’s latest attacks in southern Lebanon. [File: Menahem Kahana/AFP]

articles.title: Gaza teams recover remains of 55 people nearly 3 years after Israeli strike
articles.summary: The victims, all from one Palestinian family, had been sheltering at their family home when Israel hit it.
articles.body:
The remains of 55 Palestinians have been recovered from the rubble of a residential building in Gaza City destroyed in an Israeli air strike nearly three years ago, according to Gaza’s civil defence.

The recovery operation, which concluded on Saturday, marks the latest in a slow, largely manual campaign to retrieve the dead from beneath Gaza’s ruins. Such efforts are hampered by a chronic shortage of the heavy machinery needed to clear broken concrete.

Rescue teams said the remains were found beneath the rubble of the Malka family home, the Palestinian Wafa news agency reported.

Colonel Muhammad Abu Dan, who has been supervising the rescue teams, said they had been searching for more than 60 bodies of victims from the Malka family over the past 72 hours.

Situated in the Zeitoun neighbourhood, Israeli forces struck the building on November 19, 2023, as the family members sought shelter inside after being displaced from their own homes over the course of Israel’s genocidal war , said Wafa.

According to the United Nations Satellite Centre, 82 percent of all buildings in Gaza have been destroyed or damaged during the war.

Gaza’s Ministry of Health, along with UN agencies and aid organisations, estimate that between 10,000 and 14,000 people remain missing under rubble across the territory.

Abu Dan has called on international humanitarian organisations to provide as much equipment as possible so that his teams can recover the largest number of people possible from the rubble, as reported by Gaza’s Government Media Office.

As most of the bodies have been recovered, a joint funeral procession is expected to take place next weekend.

The recovery operation took place after United States ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee , said there was no plan to force Palestinians to leave Gaza after ⁠two Israeli ministers earlier in the week floated proposals for the mass removal of people from the besieged ⁠territory.

“I can tell you categorically there is no plan of the Israelis to displace people out of Gaza against their will,” Huckabee told reporters in ‌Turmus Ayya, a town in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.

“Nobody is suggesting that there will be forced displacement. The Israelis are not. The Americans are certainly not. ⁠I know of no one who supports that.”

Earlier this week, Defence Minister ⁠ Israel Katz said there was “no real solution for Gaza in the end without this migration”, while National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir outlined a seven-year plan for expelling Gaza’s population through what he described as “voluntary emigration”.

Meanwhile, Gaza’s Ministry of Health said hospitals in the strip received 17 bodies over the past 48 hours as well as 27 injured people, according to figures compiled from admissions.

The latest casualties included five new fatalities, one person who died from previous wounds and 11 bodies recovered from beneath debris. Additional victims remain trapped under rubble or lying in the streets, with ambulance and civil defence teams still unable to reach them, it added.

At least three Palestinians were injured in Israeli attacks on Saturday, two in an Israeli attack on a beach in the al-Khalidi area, north of Gaza City, and one in a targeted attack on the al-Sudaniyya area, northwest of Gaza City.

Since the “ceasefire” took hold last October, at least 1,344 people have been killed and 4,464 injured while at least 815 bodies have been recovered from the rubble, according to the Health Ministry.

The overall death toll since October 2023 has risen to 73,470, with at least 174,540 injured, according to the latest available figures.

articles.title: AI robot pet could know your family too well
articles.summary: The OlloNi SS1 AI robot pet uses a 4K camera and facial recognition to learn your family, but its removable Red Heart memory module raises questions.
articles.body: We've covered home robots that can fold laundry and others designed to become AI companions. Now there's one that wants to remember your family. The OlloNi SS1 is an AI robot pet that can recognize family members and pets as it moves around your home. OlloBot says it can learn your routines, respond to emotional cues and save memorable family moments along the way. Here's where it gets really interesting. OlloNi has a removable "Red Heart" memory module designed to carry those memories into a future OlloBot. So, when the robot gets replaced, years of personalization could move right along with you. I can see the appeal of that. I also think it's important to ask yourself this: How much of your family's life are you comfortable letting a robot remember? Here's how OlloNi works, what it can remember and the privacy questions to consider before deciding whether you'd want one in your home. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats , has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com WOULD YOU PAY $8,000 FOR A ROBOT TO FOLD LAUNDRY? What is the OlloNi SS1 AI robot pet? The OlloNi SS1 is OlloBot's newest AI companion robot pet, developed by Hong Kong-based Ollobot Robotics Limited. Unlike a robot built mainly for chores, the SS1 is designed to interact with the people and pets living around it. Two circular eye screens display expressions while a separate main screen handles information and direct interaction. The setup gives OlloNi a face that can react visually without relying on spoken responses every time. A 4K camera with motion tracking helps the robot recognize individual family members and household pets. OlloBot says the SS1 gradually learns routines and preferences as it spends more time with a household. It also adapts to different communication patterns. That puts OlloNi in a different category from a robot vacuum or a machine built mainly to handle physical work. The goal here is to make the robot feel increasingly familiar. OlloNi wants to understand how you are feeling OlloBot is also giving the SS1 what it describes as proactive emotional interaction. The company says the robot uses several types of information to interpret what is happening around it. That includes someone's tone of voice and facial expression. It can also learn behavioral patterns over time. For example, OlloBot says the robot may notice when someone appears to be feeling low. Instead of waiting for that person to issue a command, OlloNi could approach and initiate an interaction. We recently covered Familiar, another emotionally aware AI robot pet. That robot is also designed to learn routines and react to the people around it. OlloNi takes the idea in another direction by connecting that personalization to a memory system that can survive beyond the original robot. A 4K camera can capture family moments for you One feature I can see families using is OlloNi's 4K camera. With permission turned on, OlloBot says the SS1 can recognize moments such as laughter or celebrations and capture them automatically. Its AI-assisted Vlog feature can then edit the footage and add music to create home videos. I like the idea behind this. When something memorable happens, someone usually reaches for a phone. That often means the person recording ends up watching part of the moment through a screen. OlloNi could change that. Because the robot is already moving around the home, it could capture moments while everyone else stays in them. But this is also where I would start thinking seriously about privacy. You are allowing a connected 4K camera to move around your home and decide which moments may be worth saving. That is a lot of access to give any device, no matter how cute the robot looks. OlloNi can become a moving window into your home OlloNi also supports remote viewing and two-way voice and video calls. Unlike a camera sitting on a shelf, the robot can move around the home and follow activity. OlloBot says this could make remote check-ins feel more active for family members who live apart. The idea could appeal to someone who wants to stay connected with an older relative or other family members from a distance. OlloBot's website also says its app can let you see and interact with OlloNi while you are away. The app is designed to show daily moments and memories the robot has captured. However, remote access raises the stakes for security. A camera that can move around your house deserves strong account protection. Owners should know exactly who can connect to it and what happens if an account gets compromised. The Red Heart lets OlloNi's memories live on This may be the most unusual part of the SS1. OlloBot calls it the Red Heart. The detachable module has 16GB of RAM and 64GB of local storage. OlloBot says the module carries the robot's long-term memories and personalized information. Now imagine replacing the robot several years from now. Instead of starting over, OlloBot says you could move the Red Heart into a future-generation OlloBot. Family memories and personalized information could then follow you to the next device. That is a clever idea. Most gadgets become disposable once their hardware gets old. OlloBot wants the relationship you developed with this one to survive the upgrade. At the same time, think about how personal that little module could become. Years of family life could potentially be tied to it. That makes the Red Heart something I would want protected every bit as carefully as the robot itself. OlloNi SS1 privacy deserves a closer look This is where I would slow down and read the fine print. OlloBot says the SS1 uses local encrypted processing and includes a physical camera cover. The company also says facial recognition and automatic family-moment capture work with your permission. Those are good things to see. Still, a robot that can move around your home, recognize faces and build memories over time deserves more than a quick glance at the privacy settings. OlloBot's current privacy policy was last updated July 6, 2026. It covers the company's store and broader Services, including device and usage information collected when people interact with those Services. The policy also says some information may be handled by outside vendors that provide services such as IT management, data analytics or cloud storage. What I want to see next is something much more specific to the SS1 itself. If this robot can recognize your family and save moments inside your home, you should know exactly where that information goes. OlloBot should explain what stays on the Red Heart, what leaves the robot and how long anything gets stored. I would also want a clear answer about deletion. If OlloNi spends years learning your routines and how your family interacts, you should be able to see what it knows and permanently erase that information when you want it gone. AI WEARABLE WATCHES YOU TO PREDICT WHAT YOU NEED OlloBot's child privacy language needs clarification There is another privacy point worth watching. OlloBot's Aug. 28 announcement lists children separated from their parents by distance among the potential users for the SS1. Meanwhile, OlloBot's current privacy policy says its "Services are not intended to be used by children". It also says the company does not knowingly collect personal information from children under the age of majority in the user's jurisdiction. That does not automatically mean there is a conflict. The current policy appears geared largely toward OlloBot's store and broader services rather than offering a detailed privacy framework specifically for the SS1. Still, OlloBot should clarify how those terms apply when a product is designed to interact with families and potentially children inside the home. Parents should not have to guess. What happens if someone gets your Red Heart? This is one of the first questions I would ask about the Red Heart: What happens if you lose it? If your family has used OlloNi for years, that little removable module could contain a very personal history of life inside your home. OlloBot says the SS1 uses local encrypted processing, which is encouraging. What I want to know is what happens when the Red Heart comes out of the robot. If someone finds or steals it, does the information remain encrypted and inaccessible? I would also want a way to remotely erase the module if it disappears. The whole appeal of the Red Heart is that families could keep it for years and move their memories into a future OlloBot. If OlloBot wants us to hold onto something that personal for that long, I want to know exactly how it will keep those memories protected. OlloNi also keeps track of its surroundings OlloNi goes beyond watching the people around it. The robot also pays attention to what is happening inside the home. OlloBot says the SS1 includes temperature and humidity sensors along with ambient light and spatial sensors. That gives the robot more context about its surroundings. The company says those sensors can help with reminders and brief activity records tied to relevant interactions rather than continuous recording. The OlloNi SS1 crowdfunding launch has been postponed If all of this has you wondering what the robot costs, there is a catch. You cannot back the planned SS1 crowdfunding campaign right now. OlloBot previously said it would launch the OlloNi SS1 globally on Kickstarter in August 2026. In July, the company narrowed that window to late August. Then the plan changed. On Aug. 28, OlloBot announced that it had postponed the crowdfunding launch. The company pointed to recent changes in the U.S. regulatory and market-access environment for robotic devices made abroad. OlloBot says it wants a clear path to market and fulfillment before moving forward. For now, the company has not announced a new crowdfunding date. OlloBot says it will share an updated timeline through its official channels once one is confirmed. So, consider the SS1 a robot to watch rather than one you can order today. What this means to you OlloNi SS1 shows how quickly the idea of a home robot is changing. We have spent years watching robots get better at physical work. Now companies want these machines to learn about the people living around them. That changes what you need to consider before bringing one home. With a robot like OlloNi, start by looking beyond the cute eyes. Find out what its camera records and who can access those recordings. Next, understand the memory system. You should know what stays locally on the robot and what gets transmitted elsewhere. Also check whether you can permanently delete information when you want it gone. Remote access deserves attention too. Look for strong account security and controls that let you shut off features you do not use. Finally, think about the lifespan of your data. The entire point of the Red Heart is to keep personalized information after you replace the robot. That makes long-term software support especially important. We recently saw why connected robots deserve scrutiny when a security report raised concerns about a Yarbo robot mower. The issues involved remote access, cameras and home-network exposure. Yarbo later acknowledged the core technical findings and began rolling out fixes. OlloBot has already said it uses local encrypted processing and includes a physical camera cover. Now I want to see the deeper security details behind those promises. We reached out to OlloBot with questions about data storage, remote access and Red Heart security but did not hear back before our deadline. MAJORITY OF YOUNG ADULTS SAY THEY ARE 'MORE CONCERNED THAN EXCITED' ABOUT AI: PEW RESEARCH Kurt's key takeaways OlloNi SS1 caught my attention because OlloBot wants this robot to become more personal the longer it lives with you. The Red Heart is the feature I keep coming back to. Instead of losing years of personalization when the hardware gets old, your family's memories could move into the next robot. I can see why that might feel special. I can also see why some people will want the exact opposite. A robot that recognizes your family and captures private moments can learn a lot about what happens behind your front door. When those memories are designed to last for years, privacy becomes part of the buying decision from day one. OlloBot's physical camera cover and local encrypted processing are good places to start. Before anyone hands over money, though, I want clearer answers about recordings and remote access. The company also needs to explain exactly what happens to information stored in the Red Heart. That does not make OlloNi a robot to fear. It makes it a robot that asks for a lot of trust. Would you want an AI pet remembering years of your family's life and carrying those memories into its next robot body, or would that feel like giving a machine too much access to your home? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com Sign up for my FREE CyberGuy Report CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Copyright 2026 CyberGuy.com. All rights reserved.

articles.title: Benton Heights residents began asking for a playground in 2012; $1 million later, the community has opened its first park, and local children helped design it
articles.summary: US News: For more than a decade, families in the Benton Heights neighbourhood of Benton Township, Michigan, watched children play in yards, on street corners a.
articles.body: For more than a decade, families in the Benton Heights neighbourhood of Benton Township, Michigan, watched children play in yards, on street corners and in schoolyards, but had no local park of their own. Residents first began formally asking for a playground in 2012, attending meetings and submitting requests as years turned into a decade without a dedicated green space. Now, after about $1 million in investment and a design process that put local kids at the table, the community has finally opened its first park: Euclid Park. As reported by the WSJM, the grand opening this week marked not just the completion of swings, slides and walking paths, but the culmination of a long, grassroots campaign by neighbours who refused to let the idea die.A neighbourhood without a parkBenton Heights is a primarily residential area in Benton Township, just outside St. Joseph and Benton Harbour in southwest Michigan. Like many older neighbourhoods, it was built with homes, schools and churches, but with limited dedicated recreational land. For years, families who wanted a park had to drive to other parts of the township or neighbouring cities.Parents and grandparents noticed what that meant in daily life: children had few safe, nearby places to play outside; and neighbours had limited opportunities to gather informally in a shared outdoor space. The neighbourhood lacked a visible “heart” where community events could take place.Starting in 2012, residents began raising the issue at township meetings, in surveys and in conversations with local officials. The request was simple: a playground and park in Benton Heights. But turning that request into reality would take far longer and require more creativity than anyone expected.Years of requests, false starts and persistenceOver the next several years, the park idea moved in fits and starts. At times, it seemed close: a potential site was identified, a concept sketch was drawn, or a grant application was submitted. Then something would happen, budget constraints, other priorities, staffing changes, and the project would stall again. Through it all, a core group of residents kept the idea alive. They attended township board meetings year after year, politely but persistently asking about the park.They also collected signatures and informal feedback from neighbours to show ongoing support, and partnered with local organisations, schools and faith groups to keep the conversation going.For many, the park became a symbol of whether the township truly valued Benton Heights as a full partner in the community.Finding the site and the fundingEventually, township officials identified a vacant parcel on Euclid Avenue as a potential park site. The land was owned or controlled by the township, making it easier to develop without complex acquisitions.It was centrally located within Benton Heights, within walking distance for many families. Funding, however, remained a challenge. The estimated cost for a modest but durable park, with playground equipment, paths, benches, lighting and landscaping, ran close to $1 million when all infrastructure and soft costs were included. The township worked to piece together money from:Capital improvement budgets set aside for parks and recreation. State and possibly federal grants for community development and outdoor recreation. Local contributions and in-kind support from partners. Slowly, the financial picture came together, allowing the project to move from concept to construction.Letting children lead the designOne of the most distinctive aspects of Euclid Park is that local children helped shape its design. Township staff and designers held workshops and informal sessions with kids from Benton Heights, asking them what they wanted in their neighbourhood park. The conversations covered: Types of play equipment, like swings, slides, climbing structures and open areas for running; features for different age groups, from toddlers to older elementary and middle-school kids; and amenities for families: benches, shade, walking paths and space for gatherings.The township's direct engagement with the children meant that the park would be representative of the people who would be most using it.It also sent a powerful message to young residents: your ideas matter, and this is your park.What Euclid Park includesWhen construction was complete, Euclid Park offered Benton Heights its first dedicated public park. Key features include:A modern playground with equipment for various age groups, designed with input from local kids. Paved walking paths that loop through the site, suitable for strollers, wheelchairs and casual exercise. Benches and seating areas where parents and grandparents can watch children play and neighbours can chat.Planting of trees, shrubs and grasses for shade, beauty and a more park-like environment. Lighting and basic infrastructure to allow for safe use into the evening and to support future events.The design is intentionally flexible, allowing the space to host informal play, small community gatherings and possibly seasonal events in the years ahead.A grand opening years in the makingIn early September 2026, the township held a grand opening celebration for Euclid Park. Residents, local officials and community partners gathered to cut the ribbon, tour the playground and mark the occasion. For many attendees, the event was emotional: a tangible answer to more than a decade of requests. Speeches highlighted: The persistence of Benton Heights residents who kept asking for a park since 2012; the importance of equitable investment across all neighbourhoods in the township; the value of involving children in planning, not just as future users but as co-designers; and children who had helped shape the park’s design were front and centre, trying out the equipment they had once only imagined.Why this park mattersOn paper, Euclid Park is a relatively small municipal project: a single neighbourhood park with a $1 million price tag. But its significance runs deeper.For Benton Heights, the park means: a long-overdue investment in a neighbourhood that has often felt neglected; a safe, nearby place for children to play, exercise and spend time outdoors; and a new community hub where neighbours can meet, strengthening social ties and local identity. Research shows that access to parks and green space improves physical health, mental well-being and social cohesion, especially in communities that have historically had fewer amenities. Euclid Park brings those benefits directly to Benton Heights.A model for community-driven planningThe Euclid Park project shows what happens when neighbours simply refuse to give up. Persistent grassroots pressure can turn an abandoned lot into a thriving public space, even if it takes years of pushing. By letting local kids help design the playground, the town created something the community feels genuine pride in. Benton Heights leaders hope this is just the beginning.Now the hope is that this victory can be leveraged to inspire broader improvements, better street lighting, safer roads, better housing. But maintaining that momentum will require sustained effort, staying on top of maintenance, hosting neighbourhood events, listening to how residents actually use the space. For local kids, Euclid Park is already a favourite spot to run around and unwind. For their parents and grandparents, it’s living proof that relentless, year-after-year persistence really can turn a vacant lot into something special.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Colorado man who was free on bond in wife’s alleged killing is jailed after hit-and-run
articles.summary: A man in Colorado who had been free on $3 million bond in his wife’s alleged killing was arrested Friday after prosecutors said he got in a hit-and-run crash with two other vehicles in Denver.
articles.body: BOULDER, Colo. — A man in Colorado who had been free on $3 million bond in his wife’s alleged killing was arrested Friday after prosecutors said he got in a hit-and-run crash with two other vehicles in Denver. Barry Morphew was booked into the Boulder County Jail. Alamosa County District Judge Amanda Hopkins set a hearing to discuss Morphew’s bond Tuesday, online records show. Under the terms of his bond set last year, Morphew was not supposed to travel away from home in southern Colorado except for work and other limited circumstances. He got into the crash involving two other vehicles during a trip to Denver International Airport on Aug. 28, possibly to pick up his daughter, prosecutors said in a court filing. “To go to the airport for any purpose other than work constitutes a breach of his bond,” read the filing by District Attorney Anne Kelly. Morphew’s attorneys didn’t immediately respond to phone and email messages seeking comment Friday. Morphew has pleaded not guilty and faces trial next summer in the death of his wife, who disappeared in 2020. Suzanne Morphew’s skeletal remains were found off a dirt road in southern Colorado in 2023. By then, charges against Barry Morphew had been dropped, but he was charged again with first-degree murder in his wife’s death and arrested. Investigators found no sign of trauma in Suzanne Morphew’s remains but allegedly found traces in her bone marrow of a drug cocktail used to tranquilize wildlife. Barry Morphew was the only person in the area other than wildlife officials with authorization to use the chemicals, prosecutors allege.

articles.title: Florida woman who shot Army veteran over Walmart parking space will not face charges under Stand Your Ground law
articles.summary: US News: A Florida woman, Melissa Payne, will not face charges for fatally shooting Army veteran Bart Diguglielmo over a parking dispute, as prosecutors find her actions justified under the Stand Your Ground law.
articles.body: A Florida woman who fatally shot a 62-year-old Army veteran during a dispute over a Walmart parking space will not be charged after prosecutors determined she was protected by the state’s Stand Your Ground law.Melissa Payne shot Bart Diguglielmo in the abdomen during the June 30 confrontation in North Lauderdale, according to the Broward County State Attorney’s Office. Diguglielmo was unarmed.Prosecutors said they reviewed security footage, cellphone video and police body-camera recordings before concluding that Payne’s use of deadly force could not be disproved as self-defence under Florida law.According to the State Attorney’s Office, video showed Diguglielmo repeatedly approaching Payne and circling her vehicle during the argument. The dispute began after both claimed the same parking space.Under Florida’s Stand Your Ground law, a person does not have to retreat before using deadly force if they reasonably believe they face an imminent threat of death or serious bodily harm, according to the state statute.A 2017 amendment requires prosecutors to establish by “clear and convincing evidence” that the use of force was not legally justified.Assistant State Attorney Stephen Zaccor said prosecutors could not meet that standard in Payne’s case.“The video does not demonstrate that [Payne] was in the right, rather it demonstrates that the State of Florida cannot overcome her claim that she was in reasonable fear of great bodily harm by clear and convincing evidence,” Zaccor wrote in a case-closing memo.Payne told police that Diguglielmo had threatened to damage her vehicle and continued approaching her despite being told to back away, according to audio recorded by an officer’s body camera.“He’s made several threats about doing something to my vehicle,” Payne said, according to the recording. She also said she had driven around the parking lot and repeatedly asked Diguglielmo to back up before firing.Payne was arrested after the shooting, placed in handcuffs and later released, according to the case records.The decision has drawn criticism from Diguglielmo’s family. Melissa Rodriguez, an attorney representing his daughter, Amanda, told NBC 6 South Florida that the family was disappointed Payne would not face charges.Rodriguez said references to possible damage to a vehicle or other property did not establish reasonable grounds for using deadly force.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Volunteers from multiple countries join Nepal animal rescue effort
articles.summary: South Asia News: DEHRADUN: As rescue agencies continue searching for people in flood-hit areas of Nepal, animal welfare groups are running a parallel operation to resc.
articles.body: DEHRADUN: As rescue agencies continue searching for people in flood-hit areas of Nepal, animal welfare groups are running a parallel operation to rescue stranded animals, provide medical aid, and safely dispose of carcasses to prevent health risks.TFC (Thanks For Caring) Nepal, Pawdessy Nepal, and Karmayog Foundation are among the organisations involved in the effort.TFC Nepal, whose volunteers include people from India, Germany, and several other countries, has so far rescued around 15 dogs. Some were found stranded on balconies of houses buried under silt after their owners died or went missing.Tula Ram Rajbanshi, founder of TFC Nepal, told TOI from Kathmandu that the rescued dogs were being given primary medical care before being brought to Kathmandu for better shelter and treatment.“Just like humans, the animals who survived the disaster are in extreme trauma. They are still scared and avoid going near people. But they are injured and need medical care. Our volunteers are somehow managing to rescue them and provide the required treatment in these challenging times,” Rajbanshi said.He said a team of around 12 volunteers left for flood-affected Rasuwa and nearby areas on Saturday to locate and bury animal carcasses. The team had collected essential material, including PPE kits, on Friday.“Just like decomposing human bodies, the carcasses could pose a health risk to survivors. We will locate them and ensure they are properly buried,” Rajbanshi said.Meanwhile, Karmayog Foundation, which has been involved in relief work in flood-hit areas for the past few days, is arranging food for animals, said Saurav Rimal of the organisation.Rimal said caring for animals was particularly important in Nepal, where dogs are revered during Kukur Tihar, a festival dedicated to them.“In our culture, we have deep respect for animals. Hence, it is our duty to stand by them in this hour of need without discrimination,” he said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 2 ‘Alligator Alcatraz’ guards charged with battery of inmate, records show
articles.summary: Two guards who worked at the former Florida Everglades detention center dubbed “Alligator Alcatraz” have been charged with battery after they allegedly struck or touched a detainee against his will, court records show.
articles.body: Two guards who worked at the former Florida Everglades detention center dubbed “Alligator Alcatraz” have been charged with battery after they allegedly struck or touched a detainee against his will, court records show. Andre Junior Seenaraine and Stephen Jordan Trejos are accused of committing battery on a Hispanic male detainee around Jan. 25, according to Collier County records. Further details about the alleged encounter were not released. Gov. Ron DeSantis said in June that the center, located at an isolated airstrip in the Everglades, was always meant to be only temporary until more permanent immigration detention centers could be secured and that federal officials now have that capacity. The detention center was fully closed in July. “It served its purpose for the time,” the Republican governor said. “The demobilization efforts at this facility are underway.” DeSantis added that “Alligator Alcatraz” has “fulfilled the role that it was designed to serve” and “today it now has zero detainees.” The migrants held there remain in federal custody, he said. Officials announced a temporary closure of the facility earlier in June and sent all of the detainees to other facilities, saying hurricane season made it unsafe to keep them in the Everglades. Immigration advocates said the tents were never safe or humane for holding people. Detainees at the facility have talked about their difficulty accessing lawyers and described poor physical conditions, including worms in the food, toilets that didn’t flush, floors flooded with fecal waste, and mosquitoes and other insects everywhere. The detention center was built by DeSantis’ administration in a matter of days and opened in July 2025. DeSantis and President Donald Trump said the detention center was critical to Republican efforts to return people in the country illegally back to their home countries. “There is no question this mission has made the state of Florida safer,” said DeSantis, noting that 21,000 people were deported through the facility. Lawyers for the immigrants at the facility said their clients suddenly started being moved to other facilities in South Florida, California, Arizona, Louisiana and Texas earlier this month, disappearing for about a week before their attorneys and families were told where they were sent. Immigrant advocates said closing “Alligator Alcatraz” does nothing to stop the harm to people who spend months in custody as their families suffer. The Florida Immigrant Coalition said the only winners were corporations and contractors who made millions of dollars in profits as Republicans pushed an immigration emergency that does not exist. DeSantis said the airstrip the facility was built around will continue to be used. In August, Miami-Dade County regained control of site.
